paragraphs: This paper examines the 1-norm support vector machine as an alternative to the standard 2-norm version for classification into two classes. Its motivation is that a familiar, successful classifier may not be the best choice when the input contains redundant noise features. The authors argue that the 1-norm formulation may offer advantages in that setting.

A second contribution concerns how to choose the classifier’s tuning parameter. Rather than computing a solution for only one parameter setting, the proposed algorithm efficiently computes the whole solution path. This path describes how the fitted classifier changes as the tuning parameter varies, making those alternatives available for adaptive selection.

The paper therefore connects a modeling choice with a practical way to explore it. The possible benefit of the 1-norm formulation motivates considering it, while the solution-path algorithm makes selecting its tuning parameter more convenient. The abstract presents the advantage over the 2-norm SVM as a qualified argument, particularly relevant to redundant noise features, rather than a universal performance claim.
neurips-2003-1-norm-support-vector-machi.tldr: The paper argues for possible benefits of 1-norm SVMs with redundant noise features and efficiently computes their full tuning-parameter solution path.

paragraphs: The paper presents a single-chip visual sensor that detects approaching collisions from outward-expanding patterns of image motion. This radial expansion provides a visual signal of an impending impact. The design draws on a model developed to explain how flies time leg extension while approaching a landing surface, translating that biological idea into analog circuitry.

The authors developed an elementary motion detector that models the bandpass behavior of cells immediately downstream of fly photoreceptors. A fabricated chip contains a 16-by-16 array of two-dimensional motion detectors on a 2.24-by-2.24-millimeter die. It uses a standard 0.5-micrometer CMOS process and consumes 140 microwatts from a 5-volt supply.

With wide-angle optics added, the tested sensor can detect collisions approximately 500 milliseconds before impact in complex real-world scenes. The result connects a biologically motivated computation with a working, low-power device. The optics are part of the stated collision-detection setup, and the reported warning time is approximate rather than a fixed guarantee for every encounter.
neurips-2003-a-low-power-analog-vlsi-vis.tldr: A fly-inspired analog vision chip detects approaching collisions about 500 milliseconds before impact with wide-angle optics while consuming 140 microwatts.

paragraphs: This paper describes the software architecture of an autonomous robot for mapping abandoned mines. The system must produce a coherent map of a large environment while also finding places the robot can traverse. Its architecture addresses these needs through a combination of two-dimensional mapping and local three-dimensional information.

The software represents its consistent two-dimensional maps as Markov random fields. It can map large mines containing many cycles, meaning that routes through the mine can reconnect. For navigation, local three-dimensional range scans provide configuration-space maps: representations of the space relevant to the robot’s possible movement. The system then uses A* search to identify navigable paths.

The authors report deployments in three abandoned mines, including two that people could not access. They describe the resulting maps as having unprecedented detail and accuracy. These deployments show the architecture being used in actual underground environments, with global mapping and local route finding serving complementary purposes. The contribution is an integrated robotic mapping system supported by field operation.
neurips-2003-an-autonomous-robotic-syste.tldr: A robotic mapping architecture combines consistent 2D maps with 3D navigation and was deployed in three abandoned mines, including two inaccessible to people.

paragraphs: Johansson displays depict a moving person using only points attached to body joints. Humans can recognize the person even when some points disappear and unrelated moving points are present. This paper develops a probabilistic method intended to reproduce that ability by detecting the body and assigning interpretations to the observed points.

The method uses a graphical model to represent the joint distribution of body-point positions and velocities. Loopy belief propagation computes a likely interpretation of the scene from these relationships. The authors also introduce a variable for the body’s centroid, giving the model an explicit representation of the body’s overall center alongside its individual parts.

Experiments on one motion-captured sequence suggest greater accuracy than a previous method based on triangulated graphical models, especially when very few body parts remain visible. The authors attribute the improvement to both the more general graph structure and, more strongly, the centroid variable. The evidence supports the usefulness of this shared body-level information in the tested sequence, with the experimental scope explicitly limited to that sequence.
neurips-2003-an-improved-scheme-for-dete.tldr: A probabilistic body-point model with a centroid variable improves detection and labeling on one tested motion sequence, especially with few visible parts.

paragraphs: Coordinating several robots requires accounting for how their decisions affect one another. This paper connects two approaches to that problem: planning with large, weakly coupled Markov decision processes and coordinating robots through market architectures. Its contribution is an algorithm that automatically designs a market architecture for a specified class of coupled decision processes.

The resulting market causes the decentralized robot system to converge to a consistent policy. The authors also establish that this policy matches the one produced by a particular centralized planning algorithm. This gives the distributed coordination process a precise connection to a centralized planning procedure, rather than leaving their relationship only as an empirical question.

The guarantee applies to the stated class of coupled decision processes and the particular centralized algorithm used in the comparison. The paper demonstrates the method in simulations of cooperative towing, path planning under a limited fuel resource, and behavior coordination in paintball. Together, these examples illustrate the approach across different coordination tasks without extending the guarantee to every multi-robot problem.
neurips-2003-auction-mechanism-design-fo.tldr: For a class of coupled MDPs, an automatically designed market makes decentralized robots converge to the policy of a particular centralized planner.

paragraphs: The paper introduces an approximation algorithm for partially observable Markov decision processes. These are decision problems in which the agent does not directly observe the full state relevant to its choices. The proposed method represents behavior using stochastic finite state controllers, which provide a finite internal structure for choosing actions under incomplete information.

The search is restricted to controllers of bounded size. This restriction makes controller size part of the planning approach: the algorithm looks for improvements within a limited representation of behavior. The authors call their method bounded policy iteration and describe it as combining useful aspects of gradient ascent and policy iteration.

From gradient ascent, the approach aims to retain efficiency and the ability to search a restricted controller space. From policy iteration, it retains reduced vulnerability to local optima. That combination matters because a compact policy search should also be able to improve the policies it finds. The stated result is an approximation method with these complementary advantages; reduced vulnerability to local optima does not establish global optimality.
neurips-2003-bounded-finite-state-contro.tldr: Bounded policy iteration searches compact stochastic controllers for partially observable MDPs, combining efficient restricted search with less vulnerability to local optima.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to choose experimental inputs so that collected data are informative about an unknown system. Its approach is Bayesian: each choice takes account of prior information, including results from earlier trials. Experimental design therefore adapts as evidence accumulates, with each new input selected using the current state of knowledge.

The selection rule maximizes mutual information between the unknown system state and its stochastic output. In plain terms, it chooses the input expected to make the response most informative about what remains unknown. The authors prove a theorem quantifying the effectiveness of this strategy and provide examples comparing adaptive selection with nonadaptive experimental designs.

One example concerns the staircase method used in psychophysics. The paper explicitly calculates its asymptotic relative efficiency and shows that this efficiency depends on the underlying psychometric function, which describes how responses vary with the experimental input. This dependence makes the comparison more specific than a blanket preference for one design: efficiency is tied to the response-generating relationship.
neurips-2003-design-of-experiments-via-i.tldr: The paper analyzes adaptive experiments that maximize expected information and shows how staircase-method efficiency depends on the underlying psychometric function.

paragraphs: The paper proposes the maximum margin criterion as a basis for feature extraction. Feature extraction constructs a representation of data for subsequent analysis or classification. The authors show that their criterion is general enough to recover linear discriminant analysis when paired with a suitable constraint, connecting the proposal to an established method.

Using a different constraint, they derive a feature extractor that does not require the within-class scatter matrix to be nonsingular. That matrix describes variation within classes, and its nonsingularity is a problematic requirement for LDA, particularly when few samples are available. The new formulation therefore addresses a specific mathematical dependency rather than simply changing the feature-extraction objective.

The paper also establishes a kernelized, nonlinear counterpart to the linear extractor. Preliminary experiments on face images indicate that the proposed extractors are efficient and stable. Those findings provide initial empirical support for the formulations, while the structural contribution is the alternative constraint that removes the stated matrix requirement and extends to a nonlinear version.
neurips-2003-efficient-and-robust-featur.tldr: A maximum-margin feature-extraction criterion yields linear and nonlinear methods that avoid LDA’s nonsingular within-class scatter requirement, with promising preliminary face-image results.

paragraphs: This paper presents a second-generation central pattern generator chip that can produce the timing needed to control a walking machine’s leg. The focus is on implementing the neural timing component in silicon and making it more versatile than the authors’ previous chip. Such timing is a component of organizing leg movement during walking.

The new device contains more silicon neurons and uses more sophisticated neuron models. These include voltage-dependent charging as well as relative and absolute refractory periods, features that affect how a neuron responds over time. The chip also provides enhanced programmability of its neural networks, broadening the configurations available within the device.

The authors describe these changes as improvements over the earlier chip and as progress toward a self-contained locomotion controller. The distinction matters: the demonstrated contribution is a more capable timing-generating device, with greater neural complexity and programmability. A fully self-contained walking controller remains the direction of development described in the abstract, rather than the completed outcome claimed for this chip.
neurips-2003-entrainment-of-silicon-cent.tldr: A second-generation silicon pattern-generator chip adds richer neurons and programmability, advancing timing control for robotic legs toward a self-contained locomotion controller.

paragraphs: Relational Envelope-based Planning addresses decision problems where computing a complete policy would take too long to be useful. A robot may face extensive sensory information, many possible situations, and uncertain action outcomes. The paper asks how such an agent can begin acting intelligently before planning over the entire problem is feasible.

The approach combines two reductions in planning burden. First, it represents the domain as a relational Markov decision process, using a small collection of probabilistic relational rules to describe structure and dynamics compactly. This representation captures relationships in the problem instead of relying on an atomic or propositionally factored description.

Second, the planner initially works within an envelope: a restricted portion of the full state space. The agent can begin acting using that limited planning scope and expand it selectively as resources become available. The two ideas address different sources of difficulty—how the problem is represented and how much of it is planned over—supporting timely action in large, stochastic domains.
neurips-2003-envelope-based-planning-in-.tldr: Relational Envelope-based Planning combines compact probabilistic rules with an expanding restricted state space so agents can act before a complete policy is available.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to turn a large music-similarity graph into locations in Euclidean space. Its graph contains 267,000 vertices for artists, albums, and tracks, connected by 3.22 million similarity edges. Once these entities have spatial coordinates, those locations can support music browsing and playlist generation.

The authors use a family of sparse multidimensional scaling methods called Rectangular Dijkstra algorithms. These methods operate on a dense rectangular portion of the distance matrix, constructed by running Dijkstra’s algorithm a constant number of times. The computation thus centers on a selected distance representation rather than requiring the entire square distance matrix as its working input.

The paper compares Landmark MDS, which uses the Nyström approximation, with a new Fast Sparse Embedding algorithm based on FastMap. Both compare favorably with Laplacian Eigenmaps in speed and embedding quality. The stated findings support this family of methods for embedding very large sparse graphs, with the music graph providing a concrete application where the resulting geometry has practical uses.
neurips-2003-fast-embedding-of-sparse-si.tldr: Sparse MDS methods embed a large music-similarity graph and compare favorably with Laplacian Eigenmaps in speed and embedding quality.

paragraphs: This paper treats the analysis of closed image curves as a problem in geometry and statistics. Its starting point is to define a space whose elements are curves satisfying specified constraints. A shape is therefore an object in a structured space, and the constraints determine which shapes belong to that space.

The authors use the differential geometry of this curve space to formulate optimization and inference problems. This matters because statistical operations can then be defined in relation to the geometry of the allowed shapes. The approach connects the representation of admissible curves with the mathematical machinery used to analyze observations of them.

Three demonstrations show the range of the framework. The paper defines and computes statistics of observed shapes, defines and learns a parametric probability model on shape space, and constructs a binary hypothesis test there. Together, these contributions extend the geometric viewpoint from describing shape collections to learning their distribution and making a statistical decision between two hypotheses.
neurips-2003-geometric-analysis-of-const.tldr: The paper uses the geometry of constrained closed-curve spaces to compute shape statistics, learn probability models, and construct a binary hypothesis test.

paragraphs: Many classifiers optimize a surrogate loss instead of directly minimizing whether predictions are right or wrong. This paper examines the statistical consequences of that choice, motivated by methods such as support vector machines, boosting, and logistic regression. The central question is how risk measured using a surrogate relates quantitatively to risk measured using classification error.

The authors establish a general relationship for nonnegative surrogate losses through a variational transformation of the loss function. This transformation is easy to compute in many applications. They show that the relationship provides nontrivial bounds under a pointwise form of Fisher consistency for classification, identified as the weakest possible loss-function condition for that result.

The paper also refines the relationship in low-noise settings and applies it to estimating convergence rates. Those applications concern function classes formed as scaled hulls of a finite-dimensional base class. The contribution links the objective used during optimization to classification performance, while making explicit the consistency condition, noise setting, and function-class structure relevant to its different results.
neurips-2003-large-margin-classifiers-co.tldr: The paper quantitatively connects surrogate-loss risk to classification-error risk, with consistency conditions, low-noise refinements, and convergence-rate applications.

paragraphs: Spectral nonlinear dimensionality reduction typically builds a neighborhood graph and obtains an embedding from eigenfunctions of a graph-derived quadratic form. This paper proposes a more general formulation based on singular value decomposition. Its minimax approach is intended to provide a more robust foundation for constructing lower-dimensional representations.

The framework builds a quadratic form from local nullspaces on the manifold. Most spectral dimensionality-reduction principles can be recovered by selecting subsets of its constraints. It also supports methods that attach additional information to graph vertices, offering discrete or continuous maps, reduced computational complexity, and protection against some instabilities associated with eigenfunction-based solutions.

The authors show that almost all dimensionality-reduction methods based on eigenvalue decomposition have a solution instability that grows faster than problem size. They report that this behavior can already appear with fewer than 100 points and can be corrected through the minimax formulation. The result makes numerical stability a concern even for small datasets, while the claimed immunity remains specific to some solution instabilities.
neurips-2003-minimax-embeddings-92c0f86e.tldr: An SVD-based minimax framework generalizes spectral dimensionality reduction and corrects a solution instability that can arise even with fewer than 100 points.

paragraphs: This paper proposes that uncertainty in classical conditioning concerns the structure of an animal’s world model as well as its parameters. Traditional accounts fit parameters within a fixed model of reinforcer delivery. The authors instead use Bayesian model averaging to represent uncertainty over alternative explanations of how reinforcement is generated.

They apply this framework to second-order conditioning and conditioned inhibition. These conditioning regimes are similar yet produce sharply different behavioral outcomes. The theory explains that divergence through the amount of experience available and the resulting support for simpler or more complex models of the experimental situation.

According to the account, limited experience favors a simpler model that introduces spurious correlations, producing second-order conditioning. Additional experience can justify a more complex model, leading to conditioned inhibition. The proposed explanation therefore connects behavioral differences to changing uncertainty about model structure. It is presented as a theoretical account of these outcomes, with Bayesian model averaging providing the mechanism for considering multiple possible models.
neurips-2003-model-uncertainty-in-classi.tldr: A Bayesian model-averaging theory explains divergent conditioning outcomes through experience-dependent support for simpler versus more complex world models.

paragraphs: This paper addresses classification when training labels describe sets of patterns rather than individual patterns. Such data are ambiguous because the available label does not directly specify the label of every member. The authors propose an algorithm for this broader form of supervision, with multiple instance learning included as a special case.

Their approach generalizes linear programming boosting. The underlying learning problem is discrete and nonconvex, so the method uses results from disjunctive programming to construct linear relaxations. A relaxation provides a more tractable version of the optimization problem, while retaining constraints that connect it to the original formulation.

The algorithm generates successively stronger relaxations rather than relying on a single fixed one. This progressive strengthening is the main computational idea: it refines the linear approximation used to address the ambiguous-label problem. The contribution is therefore both a learning formulation for set-level labels and an optimization strategy for handling its discrete structure, extending the scope of linear programming boosting to this setting.
neurips-2003-multiple-instance-learning-.tldr: A generalization of linear programming boosting learns from set-level labels by progressively strengthening linear relaxations of a discrete, nonconvex problem.

paragraphs: Likelihood-ratio classifiers can make errors because estimated models differ from the true data-generating models. One way to compensate is to adjust the likelihood ratio separately for each pair of classes. Such adjustments can produce intransitive preferences: pairwise decisions need not fit a single consistent ordering of all classes.

This paper develops corrections focused on what is necessary for perfect classification, without requiring complete correction of the likelihood ratios themselves. That distinction narrows the target to the decision being made. Although these corrections are weaker than earlier adjustments, their discontinuous functions create analytical difficulties, and the proposed schemes require several approximations.

The authors test multiple schemes on isolated-word speech recognition and UCI datasets. Their results show that the newly calculated bias terms can substantially improve classification accuracy over both the baseline and their previous results. Perfect classification describes the target motivating the corrections; the reported empirical conclusion is improved accuracy. The work illustrates how correcting a model specifically for its decisions can be useful without fully repairing its probability comparisons.
neurips-2003-necessary-intransitive-like.tldr: Decision-focused corrections to pairwise likelihood ratios can substantially improve classification accuracy without requiring complete likelihood-ratio correction.

paragraphs: This paper develops faster algorithms for high-dimensional nonparametric classification while preserving exact answers. It concentrates on k-nearest-neighbor classification and the prediction stage of support vector machines. The motivation is that computing the final answer may require less information than explicitly identifying every nearby data point.

The authors exploit a distinction between finding a set of relevant points and determining properties of that set. If the classification query only needs those properties, there may be room to reduce computation without approximating the result. They investigate that opportunity through new algorithms based on ball trees.

On real-world datasets, the reported accelerations range from twofold to one hundredfold compared with highly optimized traditional ball-tree-based nearest-neighbor methods. The results include high-dimensional datasets and retain exact answers. The contribution is therefore an empirical demonstration that changing what a search explicitly resolves can yield meaningful speedups. The reported range describes the tested datasets, rather than a guaranteed acceleration for every classification query.
neurips-2003-new-algorithms-for-efficien.tldr: New ball-tree algorithms preserve exact classification answers while reporting twofold to one hundredfold speedups on tested real-world datasets.

paragraphs: This paper tackles the removal of reverberation from speech recorded with a single microphone. Reverberation complicates uses such as robust real-world speech recognition, and a single recording channel makes the problem especially challenging. The authors identify a mismatch between speech and the assumptions used by existing blind equalization techniques.

Their proposed principle instead relies on speech’s quasi-periodicity: its approximately repeating structure. The methods learn a dereverberation filter from a large amount of speech data without prior knowledge of those data. Quasi-periodicity supplies the speech-specific property guiding this learning, replacing assumptions that the abstract says are unsuitable for speech.

The authors state that the methods can achieve high-quality dereverberation, particularly when reverberation lasts a long time. This makes the contribution both a new principle for recovering speech and a data-driven way to learn the required filter. The claimed effectiveness is especially associated with long reverberation times, and the learning approach explicitly draws on substantial speech data.
neurips-2003-one-microphone-blind-dereve.tldr: A single-microphone dereverberation method learns from speech’s quasi-periodicity and can produce high-quality results, especially with long reverberation times.

paragraphs: This paper presents a common framework for three online learning problems: classification, regression, and uni-class learning. Online learning processes examples as they arrive, so the learning procedure must operate across a sequence of observations. The authors show how these different prediction tasks can be treated within a single algorithmic view.

The framework leads to new algorithms accompanied by worst-case loss bounds. The analysis covers both realizable and non-realizable settings, distinguishing cases where the learning problem can be fit by the relevant model from cases where it cannot. Including both settings broadens the scope of the theoretical treatment beyond an assumption of perfectly compatible data.

The resulting guarantees concern hinge loss, linking the proposed algorithms to an explicit measure of prediction performance. The paper also discusses converting its main online algorithm to batch learning, where a collection of training examples is considered together. Its contribution combines a unified algorithmic treatment with mathematical loss guarantees and a connection between sequential and batch learning.
neurips-2003-online-passive-aggressive-a.tldr: A unified framework yields online classification, regression, and uni-class algorithms with worst-case hinge-loss bounds and a discussed conversion to batch learning.

paragraphs: Sparse Bayesian learning underlies relevance vector machines, using a prior over weights that encourages a sparse representation. Its usual formulation introduces one hyperparameter for each weight and applies a particular approximation instead of fully integrating over all weights and hyperparameters. The paper addresses the theoretical justification for that approximation.

The authors show that sparse Bayesian learning can be reformulated as a rigorous variational approximation to the full model. They obtain this interpretation by expressing the prior in a dual form. This changes the mathematical perspective on the procedure and supplies a principled account of an approximation previously supported by empirical success.

The reformulation also removes the need to assume hyperpriors, which are priors over the additional hyperparameters. It provides natural explanations for why sparse solutions arise in practice. The contribution is therefore explanatory as well as mathematical: it connects the operational learning method to a variational framework and clarifies the mechanism behind the compact representations it produces.
neurips-2003-perspectives-on-sparse-baye.tldr: A dual-prior formulation gives sparse Bayesian learning a rigorous variational interpretation and explains sparsity without requiring hyperpriors.

paragraphs: This paper models sequences of user activity while balancing individual differences against patterns shared across a group. A separate model for every person and a single global model represent different ways to organize that information. The authors propose a compact generative representation that combines shared behavioral structure with user-specific proportions.

The key assumption is that heterogeneous behavior can be explained by relatively few common, structurally simple patterns. These patterns may interleave randomly, with each user exhibiting them in different proportions. The resulting distributed model operates in linear time and represents activity as symbolic sequences over a finite set of states.

An empirical study using three sources of user traces indicates improved prediction performance alongside low complexity and intuitively interpretable representations. These findings support the proposed way of sharing patterns across individuals while preserving differences in their behavior. The explanation depends on the stated modeling assumption: variation among users is represented through different mixtures of a small common collection of patterns.
neurips-2003-simplicial-mixtures-of-mark.tldr: A linear-time model represents users through interleaved shared behavior patterns, with improved prediction and interpretable representations on three sources of activity traces.

paragraphs: An SVM’s decision function usually depends on only some training examples, called support vectors. This paper investigates how large that subset is for several standard SVM formulations. Rather than treating sparsity as a general property shared equally by all SVMs, it derives lower and upper bounds on the number of support vectors.

The bounds are asymptotically sharp, addressing behavior as the amount of training data grows. For Gaussian radial basis function kernels, the paper gives distinct limiting fractions: twice the Bayes risk for the L1-SVM, the probability of noise for the L2-SVM, and one for the least-squares SVM.

These results connect the retained fraction of training examples to both the SVM formulation and properties of the classification problem. In particular, a limiting fraction of one means that the least-squares formulation approaches using all training examples as support vectors in the stated setting. The conclusions describe asymptotic behavior for the specified kernel, rather than exact support-vector counts for an arbitrary finite dataset.
neurips-2003-sparseness-of-support-vecto.tldr: Sharp asymptotic bounds show that Gaussian-kernel SVM variants retain different support-vector fractions tied to Bayes risk, noise probability, or the full dataset.

paragraphs: This paper develops a real-time visual component for evaluating human–robot interaction through facial expressions. The system detects frontal faces in video and classifies them across seven categories: neutral, anger, disgust, fear, joy, sadness, and surprise. Its motivation is the rapid timescale of face-to-face communication, where useful perception must keep up with ongoing interaction.

Face detection uses a cascade of feature detectors trained through boosting. Expression recognition combines AdaBoost with support vector machines. On two publicly available datasets, seven-way forced-choice recognition for new subjects achieves 93.3% and 97% accuracy. These figures describe that specific generalization task and evaluation format.

The classifier’s outputs vary smoothly over time, which the authors identify as potentially useful for automatically representing expression dynamics. The system was also deployed and evaluated in the field to measure spontaneous expressions during human–robot interaction. The work therefore combines real-time recognition, dataset evaluation, and an applied deployment, while presenting the value of its temporal output as a potential benefit.
neurips-2003-towards-social-robots-autom.tldr: A real-time face-expression system combines boosting and SVMs, achieves high seven-way recognition accuracy on two datasets, and is evaluated in human–robot interaction.

paragraphs: This paper addresses how to train a quantum neural network, an issue the authors argue has often been skipped in earlier proposals. Quantum computation follows mechanics sufficiently different from classical computation that a training procedure needs its own justification. The paper therefore treats learning as a central part of defining the network.

The authors propose both a simple quantum neural network and a method for training it. They state that the algorithm can be shown to work in quantum systems. This connects the proposed learning procedure to the computational setting in which the network is intended to operate.

Results on several real-world datasets show that the method can train the proposed networks and has some advantages over classical learning algorithms. Those findings support the particular network-and-training combination studied here. The contribution is a concrete treatment of quantum-network training, combining a procedure compatible with quantum systems and empirical evidence of learning, with advantages described as qualified rather than universal.
neurips-2003-training-a-quantum-neural-n.tldr: The paper proposes a quantum neural network with a compatible training method and reports successful learning with some advantages over classical algorithms.
